ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Howard Hughes

code.originalText: Establishing primary care ten months after a plane crash: contamination fears with washing and avoidance, chronic pain on long-term codeine, an opioid review, hearing, weight, kidney health and safety

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care ten months after a plane crash: contamination fears with washing and avoidance, chronic pain on long-term codeine, an opioid review, hearing, weight, kidney health and safety [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants to get back to full days of work without hours of washing and checking, and without other people seeing his rituals. [S]
He is afraid that without codeine the pain from the crash will stop him working. [S]
He wants his privacy protected and nothing about his care known outside the clinic. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Howard Robard Hughes Jr. was born in Houston, Texas, on December 24, 1905, the only child of an oilman whose drill bit became the foundation of the family fortune. [D]

After an unexplained paralysis in 1919, as a boy, he developed what a state historical handbook calls a lifetime phobic regard for his health; a psychologist who studied his life after his death concluded that his fear for his health began in childhood. [D]
He suffered a nervous breakdown in 1944. [D]

On July 7, 1946, on the first flight of the XF-11 reconnaissance plane, he crashed into houses in Beverly Hills and was critically injured, with a crushed chest, a collapsed lung, multiple broken bones and second- and third-degree burns; he nearly died. [D]
Drugs for pain were first given to him after the 1946 crash; the crash left him with lingering pain and an addiction to codeine, the beginning of a lifelong dependence on painkillers. [D]

His fear of germs grew throughout his life, with efforts to protect himself from contamination from outside; a news magazine linked his celebrated fear of germs in part to the 1946 crash, which injured his lungs and left him susceptible to bronchial infection. [D]

text.paragraph: 9 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

list.item: Aviator, aircraft builder and film producer who owns and runs several companies; test-flies his own aircraft; working long irregular hours on a very large flying boat [S]
Unmarried; lives alone in a rented house with a household staff of several employees and a personal assistant; no relative is involved in his care or named in this record [S]

His staff follow written rules he has set: they wash their hands before handing him anything, pass him objects wrapped in tissue, prepare his food in a set way, and keep visitors away; he can pay for every ritual to be carried out for him [S]

Codeine: acetaminophen-codeine tablets since the crash, now 10 to 12 a day from two prescribers at two pharmacies; no other opioids, no injection, no drugs from any other source. Alcohol: rarely (AUDIT-C 1). Never smoked tobacco [S]
Eats one meal a day that he has watched being prepared, plus milk from sealed bottles; skips meals when he cannot inspect the food [S]
No firearms in the home; drives himself and still flies [S]
Strengths: engineering talent, persistence, courage as a pilot, the resources to pay for care, loyal staff, and his own wish to get back to work without the rituals [S]

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, intense and courteous; declines to shake hands and keeps his gloves on until he has washed; speech normal in rate, a little loud; mood anxious; contamination obsessions with washing, cleaning and avoidance compulsions, Y-BOCS 28 (obsessions 14, compulsions 14); he says the fears are probably excessive (good or fair insight); no hallucinations or delusions; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in all activities; spends about four hours a day on washing and checking; avoids meetings and handshakes; reaches overhead with the left arm only with pain. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-05-04; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert, intense and courteous; declines to shake hands and keeps his gloves on until he has washed; speech normal in rate, a little loud; mood anxious; contamination obsessions with washing, cleaning and avoidance compulsions, Y-BOCS 28 (obsessions 14, compulsions 14); he says the fears are probably excessive (good or fair insight); no hallucinations or delusions; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Outpatient care with weekly visits at first. Risk factors reviewed without detail: a breakdown in earlier years, opioid use disorder, chronic pain, severe OCD, isolation and anxiety. No current thoughts of suicide. Opioids are dangerous in overdose, so means safety is part of the plan: naloxone nasal spray at home with his staff taught to use it, unused codeine tablets taken to a pharmacy take-back, and buprenorphine dispensed one week at a time at first. A written safety plan was made with him, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in his phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit. [S]

tr.td: Intrusive fears of contamination by germs for about a year, worse since the crash, with hand washing, cleaning of objects and avoidance of handshakes, shared spaces and food handled by others, taking about four hours a day; he recognizes the fears are probably excessive; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his documented fear of germs; resolved into the diagnosis of OCD at the consultation. Not a claim about his real symptoms in 1947.

Opioid use disorder, moderate (four of the DSM-5-TR criteria that count for a prescribed opioid: taking more than prescribed, failed attempts to cut down, time spent getting prescriptions from two prescribers, and craving), on codeine prescribed after a crash; buprenorphine planned
S — Synthetic modern coding; tolerance and withdrawal are not counted for a medicine taken under medical supervision. Person-first language; not a claim about his real diagnosis.
Chronic pain after major trauma ten months ago (crushed chest with rib fractures, collapsed lung, other fractures and burns): chest wall, left shoulder and low back pain, PEG 6.7
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his documented injuries.
Difficulty hearing conversation, worse in noise, after years of flying in loud aircraft; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem; resolved into a diagnosis when audiometry was done at five weeks. His documented deafness is from later years.
Weight loss of about 8 kg since the crash (BMI 19.7), from eating little outside food he has prepared or inspected himself because of contamination fears
S — Synthetic nutrition problem linked to the contamination fears; not a claim about his real weight in 1947.

Psychiatry consultation to confirm the diagnosis, advise on an SSRI at OCD doses with buprenorphine, plan exposure and response prevention, and advise on how his staff can stop carrying out rituals for him. Guideline: Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (2007); Guideline Watch (March 2013): Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (Koran LM, Simpson HB), as reported by Psychiatric News (2013); Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31) (2005) [S]

Opioid review under the CDC 2022 guideline: benefits and harms reviewed with him, a prescription drug monitoring program check before every controlled-substance prescription, urine drug testing with consent and explained as part of care, one prescriber and one pharmacy, a nonjudgmental DSM-5-TR assessment for opioid use disorder, and no abrupt stop of codeine. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022); Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) (2026) [S]

Buprenorphine with naloxone for opioid use disorder and pain: induction in the clinic at one week after about 20 hours without codeine, then 8 mg twice daily, dispensed weekly at first; naloxone nasal spray at home; no benzodiazepines; leftover codeine to a pharmacy take-back. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022); The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020) [S]

Pain after major trauma: scheduled acetaminophen up to 3,000 mg a day, physical therapy for the chest wall, left shoulder and low back, graded activity, sleep, and pain coping skills woven into his therapy; no NSAID long term. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022) [S]

Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone, means safety for opioids, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Hearing: audiometry, then hearing aids and a remote microphone if hearing loss is confirmed; hearing protection when flying and in the factory. Guideline: Hearing loss in adults: assessment and management (NG98) (2018) [S]

Kidney health: creatinine, eGFR and urine albumin at baseline and a metabolic panel at follow-up while on scheduled acetaminophen and any new medicine; acetaminophen kept at or below 3,000 mg a day; no long-term NSAID. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022) [S]

Privacy: care documented in the clinic record only; letters about his health go only to people he names. Guideline: Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (2007) [S]
